Article Title: From Riyadh to Paris: How EWC's unexpected move accelerated its global plans
Article Text:
Image credit: Esports World Cup (Image credit: Vineet Ramakrishnan/TimesofIndia.com)

TimesofIndia.com in PARIS:

Faisal Bin Homran, chief product officer of the Esports Foundation (Image credit: Vineet Ramakrishnan/TimesofIndia.com)

(Image credit: Vineet Ramakrishnan/TimesofIndia.com)

The Esports World Cup was not supposed to be in Paris this year. The 2026 edition was moved from Riyadh to the French capital in May amid the regional security situation, with the Esports Foundation stressing that Riyadh remained the event's home.What was initially a necessity has now given the organisers something else to think about: whether EWC can actually travel. Faisal Bin Homran, chief product officer of the Esports Foundation, says the Paris move has accelerated a plan to eventually take the tournament to other cities.For Bin Homran, that has provided something more useful than a change of venue: proof that the tournament can travel.“What happened this year is we expedited this move,” Bin Homran told TimesofIndia.com. “It was 2028, 2029, 2030. To rotate, it was 2036. So we expedited this strategy. Was it 2026 planned? No. But this move was expedited. And this tells me that it's ready to move around.”The Paris edition, therefore, is being viewed inside the Foundation as more than an international stop for an event whose home has been Riyadh.“I think we would see EWC rotating. We don't know where or when yet. But I think at the end of it, it would be a global IP event in the world,” he said.Riyadh will continue to be the event's hub, even as EWC looks to take the tournament to other cities.“Adding to that, Riyadh would be the hub and the host of it as a default,” Bin Homran said.Paris had the practical ingredients to make the move possible. Bin Homran pointed to the city's infrastructure and existing esports audience, as well as its recent experience hosting major esports tournaments.The biggest logistical problem was not the venue. “The visa was a challenge, to be honest,” he said.The Foundation had less than six weeks to put the Paris edition together and needed a large number of visas to be issued. Bin Homran credited support from France and Paris for helping the event overcome that hurdle.“So it was tough. But we overcome it with the partnership with them.”The move also appears to have sharpened the Foundation's thinking about what EWC is supposed to become. Bin Homran does not describe it simply as a tournament. He keeps returning to four principles: the best games, the best clubs and players, and a gaming festival that can attract people beyond the core esports audience.“We have the best games around the world. We have the best clubs and the best players. And we have the best gaming festival. So it is a festival that hosts the best tournaments from all over the world.”In Paris, EWC has also been built around more than the competition, with fan zones and activities running alongside the tournaments. Bin Homran said the idea is to draw people beyond those who follow individual esports titles.“There is something for families to come into it. There is something for esports fans. And there is something for gamers, which is a wider appealing audience than esports fans' niche who are only watching Fnatic to play Valorant or watching Magnus and just all these.”The ambition is now to take that product to more markets and India is one of them.Bin Homran described India as “one of the most important markets” because of its player base, games and influencer culture. But he also pointed to a problem that has less to do with the size of the country's gaming audience and more to do with how the global games industry operates.“We had some challenges of some games that has a different version in India,” he said. “I hope that publishers fix this.”His preference is for games to be more globally aligned so that players from different markets can compete against one another without separate versions creating barriers.“If publishers globalise their games, that would help me,” he said. “I don't want to have, oh, when I play, I want to talk, I want to talk with one language. Let's play with the mobile. Let's play this game. Let's play this game.”The Foundation is already researching how it can increase its presence in India, including through qualifiers and tournaments. And Bin Homran has a specific idea for what that could look like.“My goal, hopefully one day, to have a qualifier in each of the different main markets. So I want the qualifier to be physical there. So you have road to EWC India.”The idea is straightforward: a physical Indian qualifier focused on Indian players and clubs, with the winners earning a route to the Esports World Cup.“This is to see which Indian club or players qualify to EWC,” he said. “It's similar to this. But it's only focusing on the Indian players and Indian clubs. That's the aim and the goal. And we're working towards that goal.”The Foundation is already looking at ways to increase its presence in India, including qualifiers and tournaments. Bin Homran has a specific idea in mind.Bin Homran also rejected the idea that India lacks the ingredients to produce more top-level esports participation. “I don't think there's something missing in India,” he said, adding, “I think it's the alignment of the main stakeholders. Because I own EWC. I don't own publisher's license.”He believes that situation is changing as publishers look at how to globalise their games and improve their presence in India. “So as soon as everything is aligned, I think we can do it faster than ever,” he said.The India plans are still being worked on. There is no city, date or tournament format announced in the interview. But Bin Homran said the Foundation is researching how to build a stronger presence in the country and hopes to have more activity there soon.“I hope one day or soon, we will have more stuff there,” he said. “And I will go myself there and see it and check it out.”For now, Paris is serving a similar purpose for EWC itself. The Foundation has taken a tournament that was built around Riyadh and put it in a different city, with a different audience and a compressed preparation timeline.Bin Homran's assessment is that the experiment has worked well enough to accelerate an ambition that had been further down the road. The next destination is not decided. But the direction is.“I think we would see EWC rotating,” Bin Homran said. “We don't know where or when yet.” And somewhere in that future rotation, the Foundation wants India to have its own route in. “Road to EWC India.”
Article Summary: The 2026 edition was moved from Riyadh to the French capital in May amid the regional security situation. Faisal Bin Homran, chief product officer of the Esports Foundation, says the Paris move has accelerated a plan to eventually take the tournament to other cities.

Article Title: India play 600th Test at Galle: What happened in 1st, 100th, 200th, 300th, 400th and 500th Tests?
Article Text:
(clockwise from top left): Dravid, Yuvraj and Kaif after Jamaica Test; Brian Lara falls; R Ashwin in Kanpur; Mohammed Shami after his wicket of Mark Craig in Kanpur; A picture of All India Cricket side which played first Test in 1932.

India's first Test: England vs India, Lord's, June 25 - 28, 1932

India's 100th Test: India vs England, Birmingham, July 13 - 15, 1967

India's 200th Test: India vs Pakistan, Lahore, December 10 - 15, 1982

India's 300th Test: India vs South Africa, Ahmedabad, November 20 - 23, 1996

India's 400th Test: West Indies vs India, Sabina Park, Jamaica, June 30 - July 02, 2006

India's 500th Test: India vs New Zealand, Green Park, Kanpur

Ninety-four years after Colonel Cottari Kanakaiya Nayudu (CK Nayadu) led a motley crew of a resurgent nation in their first Test match at Lord's Cricket Ground on June 25 1932, India will play their 600th game in the cricket's oldest and toughest format at Galle International Stadium in Sri Lanka on Saturday.The men-in-Blue, led by Shubman Gill, are set to become only the third team after England and Australia to reach the milestone, that too on the day when the nation is celebrating its 80th Independence Day from the colonial rule.A total of 319 lucky players have donned the India cap in Tests so far, Manav Suthar being the latest among them, and Sachin Tendulkar holds the record of most Test caps - 200.From Colonel C K Nayadu to Rishabh Pant, Indian men's cricket team have been led by 38 captains in these ninety-four years, under whom they have been through the lowest of lows to the highest of highs but constantly aspiring to be better.Virat Kohli holds the record for captaining India in the most Test matches, having led the team in 68 Tests from 2014 to 2022. Under his leadership, India secured 40 wins, making him also India's most successful Test captain.As India are set to create history at Galle, here’s a look at India’s 1st, 100th, 200th, 300th, 400th nd 500th match:The Maharajah of Porbandar was named captain of the touring Indian side but good sense prevailed and CK Nayadu was nominated to lead the side in India's first-ever Test, however not before some off-field drama.England captain Douglas Jardine rescued his side after Mohammad Nissar rocked England as he clean bowled Percy Holmes and Herbert Sutcliffe, on 6 and 3, respectively.Jardine's 79 and Les Ames' 65 took England to 259 in the first innings. Nasser (93/5) took India's first five-wicket haul in Tests.India were bowled out for 189 in their first innings as Bill Bowes (49/4) and Bill Voice (23/3) ran through Indian batting, giving England a lead of 70 runs, which they capitalized on, and declared their second innings at 275/8.India had 346 runs to chase and England easily won the match by 158 runs despite Amar Singh's (51) gutsy knock.Led by one of India's greatest Test captain, Mansur Ali Khan Pataudi, India toured England England for a three-match Test series.Having lost the first two Tests, India entered the third match looking to avoid a series whitewash.England won the toss and scored 298 in the first innings. India's four spinners — Srinivas Venkataraghavan, Bhagwath Chandrasekhar, Bishan Bedi and Erapalli Prasanna — took all 10 English wickets.India's batting line-up featured Farokh Engineer, Ajit Wadekar, Chandu Borde and Pataudi, but the visitors struggled against the England attack. India were bowled out for just 92, with only four batters reaching double figures. Engineer was the top scorer with 23.Chandrasekhar, Bedi and Prasanna then took nine of England's 10 second-innings wickets. However, England had already built a lead of more than 400 and set India a target of 410.Wadekar scored 70, but India were dismissed for 277. England won by 132 runs and completed a 3-0 series sweep.Their was no Covid-19 in 1982, but there were no spectators in Lahore's historic Gaddafi Stadium to see the Test match as the Pakistan Cricket Board - then Board of Control for Cricket in Pakistan (BCCP), had sold the entire series to a private party for around £800,000. The contractor set high entry prices, keeping many spectators away. The rates were cut by half after the second day, but the crowds did not return.The match, first of the six-Test series, had some terrific performances from batsmen of both sides. Zaheer Abbas played a monstrous knock of 215 runs, which was also his 100th first class ton, as Pakistan finished their first innings at 485, after being asked to bat by Indian captain Sunil Gavaskar.Returning to the side after nearly two years, Mohinder Amarnath led India's reply with an unbeaten knock of 109 runs. Sunil Gavaskar also scored 81, and passed the 7,000 Test run mark, while Sandeep Patil played a quickfire knock of 68 off 56 balls. India scored 379 in their first innings.Pakistan scored 135/1 in their second innings, and the match ended in a draw.It was the first Test of the three-match series against South Africa, and VVS Laxman also made his Test debut in this match. India captain Sachin Tendulkar put India into advantagious position by batting first on a brown, dusty pitch.Tendulkar's 42, Manjrekar's 34, Azharuddin's 35 helped India reach 223 in their first innings even as Allan Donald took 37 for 4.India however hit back with spin and the then trio of Anil Kumble, Sunil Joshi and Narendra Hirwani scalped 8 South African wickets, and South Africa could take just 21-run lead.India struggled again with the bat and were reduced to 123/6 in their second innings. Laxman scored 51 and helped India reach 190.South Africa needed 170 to win but lost two wickets without adding a run to the scoreboard. Javagal Srinath then took six wickets as South Africa were bowled out for 105.All previous three of the Tests in the series had ended in a draw and both teams reached Sabina Park for the last Test.Brian Charles Lara's side were bundled out for a mere 103 with Harbhajan Singh (13/5) being the wrecker-in-chief.Rahul Dravid, India's captain, won the toss and chose to bat. India struggled with the bat again, but Dravid scored 81 as they made 200.India had a 97-run lead but could not build a big advantage with the bat. Dravid again led the way, scoring 68 as India were dismissed for 171. West Indies were set 269 to win. Anil Kumble took six wickets as India bowled them out for 219.India won by 49 runs in their 400th Test.India reached Kanpur's iconic Green Park stadium to play the 500th Test, led by Virat Kohli. It was the first Test of three-match series.The Test match was being played at the time when India were at peak of their home domination with Ashiwn and Jadeja at their best. Murali Vijay (65), and Cheteshwar Pujara's (62) half-centuries took India to 318 in the first innings on a decent pitch.While Tom Latham (58), New Zealand captain Kane Williamson (75), and Luke Ronchi (38) played promising knocks as Black Caps batted for almost 96 overs, Jadeja (73/5), and Ashwin (93/4) made sure India had a lead of 56 runs.Four Indian batters - Vijay, Pujara, Rohit Sharma, and Jadeja - scored fifties in the second innings as India declared at 377/5 on day 4, setting an improbable target of 434 runs for New Zealand.Of course Ravichandran Ashwin finished the job in the fourth innings, taking a six-wicket haul, and India scripted a famous win by 197 runs at Green Park.India went on to win the series 3-0.
Article Summary: India will play their 600th Test match at Galle International Stadium in Sri Lanka on Saturday. The men-in-Blue are set to become only the third team after England and Australia to reach the milestone. A total of 319 lucky players have donned the India cap in Tests so far, and Sachin Tendulkar holds the record of most Test caps.

Article Title: India's red-ball reset: Shubman Gill leads India into 600th Test against spin-heavy Sri Lanka
Article Text:
Shubman Gill and Dhananjaya de Silva (Image credit: Sri Lanka Cricket)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

As India prepare to play their landmark 600th Test, the setting could hardly be more fitting. The first Test against Sri Lanka, beginning on Saturday, coincides with India’s 80th Independence Day and will be played at Galle International Stadium, itself celebrating a milestone by hosting its 50th Test. Nestled beside the Indian Ocean and overlooked by the iconic 17th-century Portuguese fort, Galle has long been Sri Lanka’s spin fortress.India, meanwhile, arrive seeking not just a series win but a revival of their fading Test fortunes after an inconsistent year under coach Gautam Gambhir. Leading India in the historic Test is skipper Shubman Gill, who described the occasion as a “huge honour”.“Leading my country in our 600th Test is a big honour and privilege for me and doing that on Independence Day is even more special,” Gill said on Friday.Only England (1,097) and Australia (883) have played more Tests than India. Since beginning their Test journey at Lord’s in 1932, India have won 186 matches, lost 188 and drawn 224, with one famous tie.The significance of the occasion, however, is matched by the challenge facing Gill’s men. India have slipped to fifth in the World Test Championship standings after losing 10 of their 20 Tests under Gambhir.With only nine Tests remaining before the next WTC final cycle concludes, Gill knows there is little room for error.“The main goal is to play the WTC final next year. We probably need to win six or seven of our remaining Tests to have a good chance,” the Indian captain said.Selection remains one of the key talking points. Going by Gill’s comments on Friday, Prasidh Krishna appears set to partner Mohammed Siraj with the new ball ahead of rookie pacer Gurnoor Brar. While Gill praised Gurnoor’s ability to extract bounce and make an impact with the old ball, he hinted that Prasidh’s recent form may have given him the edge.On a pitch expected to aid spin as the game progresses, India are likely to field a three-pronged left-arm spin attack comprising Ravindra Jadeja, Kuldeep Yadav and Manav Suthar.
Article Summary: India face Sri Lanka in their landmark 600th Test on Saturday. The first Test coincides with India’s 80th Independence Day. The match will be played at Galle International Stadium, itself celebrating its 50th Test. Only England (1,097) and Australia (883) have played more Tests than India.

Article Title: Rishabh Pant can make Virender Sehwag-like impact: Angelo Mathews
Article Text:
Rishabh Pant (Getty Images)

'Lack of Test opportunities disheartening'

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Sri Lanka's last Test win against India came under Angelo Mathews in 2015 in Galle—the venue for the first Test starting on Saturday. He was a new captain thenWhile all the talk leading up to the series has been around spinners playing the key role, Mathews highlighted that playing rank turners can backfire on home teams."If I am not mistaken, India played on quite a few ranked turners against New Zealand and South Africa. Sometimes, it could backfire. We played on ranked turners against foreign teams and it has backfired for us as well. Because it's not easy as a batsman to play on ranked turners no matter how good you are," Mathews told TOI on Friday.Mathews has been a part of a Sri Lankan team which had heady battles with India, especially on their own turf. He believes a player like Rishabh Pant should be backed by the management as he too could have an impact like Virender Sehwag did in Sri Lanka."I remember when Ajanta Mendis was running through the Indian batting line-up, Sehwag was the one standing tall. He was so destructive and such a disruption. Pant is such a player," Mathews said."Pant takes the game on as soon as he walks into the crease. So, bowlers, watch out. A player like that needs backing. A guy like that who can take the game away within a few hours should be backed," he added.A big part of succeeding in Sri Lanka is to be measured against playing spin.One can't afford to go into his shell. "It's about being proactive. I think if you are sweeping, sweep well. If you are using your feet, use your feet well. So, it's all about using your feet and also knowing your options of how to score runs on those wickets is going to be crucial.Mathews also stressed on the importance of not just focusing on spinners in Sri Lanka. "It's definitely not wise to believe that cricket in Sri Lanka will be dictated only by spin," he said. "I wouldn't rule out the faster bowlers also because they are skillful. Guys like Asif Fernando and Vishwa Fernando have a bigger role to play as well, especially with the new ball," he added.Sri Lankan cricket saw a sharp drop in the number of Test matches they played after the stalwarts like Kumar Sangakkara and Mahela Jayawardene retired. For Mathews, it is a big reason behind Sri Lanka's inconsistent performances."I don't think poor performance or whatever has to do anything with that. It's just that it's disappointing that the so-called big teams or who is not wanting to play too many matches against Sri Lanka is quite disheartening. And I think ICC has a bigger role to play in this," Mathews opined."We have not been consistent throughout which can happen to any team. The more we play, the more we learn. We are playing Test matches one year apart. Sri Lanka Cricket can discuss with ICC and other boards as well and try to accommodate more Test cricket," he added.Watch Sri Lanka vs. India 1st Test Day 1 on August 15, 2026, from 10 AM IST live on Sony Sports Ten 1 SD & HD and Sony LIV.
Article Summary: Sri Lanka's last Test win against India came under Angelo Mathews in 2015 in Galle. Mathews believes a player like Rishabh Pant should be backed by the management. Sri Lanka cricket saw a sharp drop in the number of Test matches they played after stalwarts like Kumar Sangakkara and Mahela Jayawardene retired.

Article Title: Harmanpreet Singh's men eye end to 51-year jinx as India begin World Cup campaign
Article Text:
FIH Hockey World Cup 2026: Harmanpreet Singh-led India eye new chapter

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India celebrates its 80th Independence Day on Saturday, some 6,300 km away in Amstelveen, Harmanpreet Singh and his men will take their first step towards breaking a 51-year jinx at the FIH World Cup.When the national anthem is played at the Wagener Hockey Stadium before India’s campaign opener against Wales, the players will experience familiar goosebumps. But this time, there will also be a heightened sense of responsibility, with the significance of the day weighing heavily on the occasion.This World Cup is unlike the previous two editions, both staged in Odisha, where home support and emotion ran high. While this tournament is being billed as India’s best chance to end their five-decade wait for a World Cup medal, the numbers suggest there is plenty of ground to cover.India endured an underwhelming start to the FIH Pro League before finding their feet towards the business end of the tournament. Their world ranking has also slipped sharply, with the team currently eighth in the charts.It is difficult to discuss India’s World Cup campaign in the Netherlands and Belgium without mentioning the jersey-colour controversy, which has taken considerable attention away from the team and the tournament.The decision to move away from the traditional blue has embroiled Indian hockey in a needless controversy and, unfortunately, dragged the players into it.The explanation that the colour change was based on scientific considerations to improve ball visibility against the blue turf has further put the team under scrutiny. Any slip-up on the field could once again invite questions over the decision.That said, India, drawn alongside Wales, England and Pakistan in Pool D, will face their sternest test in the opening phase against England, ranked third in the world behind co-hosts Belgium and the Netherlands.India will be expected to come through against Wales and Pakistan and advance to the next stage, where the real challenge could begin against formidable opponents such as Olympic champions Netherlands and Argentina, provided both live up to expectations.
Article Summary: India face Wales, England and Pakistan in Pool D of the 2026 FIH World Cup. Harmanpreet Singh's men have not won a World Cup medal in 51 years. India endured an underwhelming start to the FIH Pro League before finding their feet.

Article Title: IND vs SL 1st Test: India may unleash three left-arm spinners in Galle as Morkel drops big hint
Article Text:
Ravindra Jadeja, front left, and Manav Suthar, front right, during a practice session. (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India could field three left-arm spinners, with Ravindra Jadeja Kuldeep Yadav and Manav Suthar all in contention for the first Test against Sri Lanka in Galle.As expected, the Galle International Stadium pitch underwent a ‘haircut’ on Wednesday, three days before the Test. With the surface expected to favour spin as the match progresses, India’s bowling coach Morne Morkel dropped a strong hint that the three left-armers could be India’s preferred spin combination.“Kuldeep is there and he’s an attacking sort of bowler. For us, his experience and class can’t be overlooked. They’re all different in their own way — one (Suthar) turns it a bit more, one (Jadeja) is slightly more accurate. I don’t think three left-arm spinners are a massive concern for us. It’s about how (captain Shubman) Gill uses them at certain times. In terms of skill, they have what it takes to get 20 wickets for us,” Morkel told reporters in Galle on Thursday.Jadeja is an automatic pick, while Suthar impressed in the recent tour game in Sri Lanka. Kuldeep, meanwhile, is a left-arm wrist-spinner.The pitch had a brownish look two days before the Test and is expected to offer good batting conditions initially before turning increasingly.“For sure, it’s a good-looking surface. I’d be slightly surprised if it goes the other way. Traditionally, at this venue, the first two days belong to the batting side, or your first innings.So that will be important to whatever happens at the toss. If you bat first, make sure you go big; if you bowl first, get the ball in the right areas,” Morkel said.India could also opt for three pacers — Mohammed Siraj , Prasidh Krishna and Gurnoor Brar, who took 10 wickets for India ‘A’ during their shadow tour of Sri Lanka last month and is in line for his Test debut.Morkel said the heat, humidity and the Kookaburra ball going soft early would test India’s quicks. He urged them to bowl short, high-intensity spells and make the most of the conditions. “It’s about the mindset. As a fast bowler, if you’re going to bowl short spells, put energy into the ball and hit good areas, you’ll always have an opportunity,” he said.Morkel also stressed the need for India’s quicks to be “street-smart” once the ball loses its hardness.
Article Summary: India could field three left-arm spinners against Sri Lanka. Ravindra Jadeja, Kuldeep Yadav and Manav Suthar all in contention. The Galle International Stadium pitch underwent a ‘haircut’ on Wednesday.

Article Title: Afghanistan Cricket Board wants India T20I shifted to festival date
Article Text:
Representative Image: Afghanistan cricketers (AP Photo)

MUMBAI: The Afghanistan Cricket Board (ACB) has approached the BCCI with a request to move one of the three T20Is against India in Sept to Sept 14, coinciding with Ganesh Chaturthi , TOI has learnt.The series is currently scheduled to be played in New Delhi on Sept 13, 15 and 17. Sources familiar with the developments said the ACB has asked if either the first or second game could be moved to Sept 14 as “a special gesture” and to add a festive touch to the growing cricketing ties between the two countries.“As a part of a special gesture, the ACB is considering Sept 14 as one of the match dates for the India-Afghanistan T20I series, coinciding with Ganesh Chaturthi, one of India’s most widely observed and auspicious festivals. If confirmed, the fixture could add a distinctive cultural dimension to the series and create a special occasion for cricket fans around the country,” ITW Universe, which is handling the series’ media rights, on-ground branding and production, said in a release.All three matches, which are to be hosted by the ACB, will be played in New Delhi.
Article Summary: Afghanistan Cricket Board (ACB) has approached the BCCI with a request to move one of the three T20Is against India in Sept to Sept 14, coinciding with Ganesh Chaturthi. The series is currently scheduled to be played in New Delhi on Sept 13, 15 and 17.

Article Title: ‘Be yourself, trust yourself’: The mental mantra driving India’s women hockey team
Article Text:
Indian women’s hockey team

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

As the Indian women’s hockey team puts the finishing touches to their preparations ahead of the World Cup, one individual has been making a difference off the field.Ben Wienk describes himself as a ‘Human Sports Innovator,’ and is helping the players understand themselves better and, in the process, discover their “unseen potential” — qualities that can ultimately help them perform better.“The goal is not for me to understand the player completely. I want her to understand herself better. What gives me energy? What matters to me? When do I feel confident? How do I learn best? What are my natural strengths? And what happens to me when the pressure increases?” Wienk, mental conditioning coach in the women’s hockey set-up, told TOI.And to do all this, he uses methods such as “profiling, personal conversations, observations and, above all, real-life situations”.It is not only about helping the players understand themselves better. Wienk’s work also gives head coach Sjoerd Marijne a better understanding of how to deal with each player.“Maybe if I shout at one player, she freezes and it doesn’t work. I may have to be more friendly with her. With another player, maybe I have to shout because that works for her,” Marijne said.Wienk further explained saying, “A coaching message can work immediately for one player while creating uncertainty in another.One player needs short, concrete information, while another first wants to understand the bigger picture.”Therein lies the importance of his role. In a team where players come from different backgrounds and with different personalities, there is no one-size-fits-all approach. The idea is not to make everyone think or respond in the same way. It is to understand what makes each player tick and find the best way to bring out her strengths.It’s challenging, but that is precisely what attracted Wienk to the assignment in the first place.“This assignment brings so many different elements together: elite sport, different personalities and backgrounds, a fascinating culture, and at the same time the ambition to perform at the very highest international level,” said the Dutchman.And when he first started working with the team, he was impressed by what he saw.“The first thing that struck me was the enormous drive and willingness to work hard. There is a great deal of ambition within this group,” he said.That ambition has taken the team forward this year. India qualified for the World Cup, showed encouraging signs in Argentina and Australia and then went on to win the Nations Cup. But the World Cup is a different ball game, and that’s where Wienk’s work could be put to its biggest test.Wienk is not trying to remove pressure from the players. Instead, he wants them to understand what happens to them when the pressure increases. “The goal is not for a player to suddenly become someone else under pressure. The goal is for her to know herself well enough to stay close to her own strengths under pressure while continuing to trust her teammates,” he said.And the players, too, appear to be enjoying the process.“We worked on trusting and communicating with each other and building a connection within the team. I particularly enjoyed the blindfold exercise, where we had to guide each other. It showed us how important it is to trust our teammates and react quickly to their calls,” said Shilpi Dabas, one of the newcomers in the team.The real test, however, will come when India walk out for their World Cup opener against China on Sunday. Wienk has a simple message for them.“Be yourself. Trust yourself. Trust each other. And do it together.”The World Cup is only the first of two major challenges, with the Asian Games to follow soon after. For Wienk, the way to deal with that pressure is equally simple: “Keep the ambition big, but the daily task small.”For now, the task is the World Cup. And for India, the hope is that understanding themselves — and each other — a little better will help them make the most of what they already have.
Article Summary: Ben Wienk is a mental conditioning coach in the Indian women's hockey team. He is helping the players understand themselves better and discover their ‘unseen potential’ He uses methods such as ‘profiling, personal conversations, observations and, above all, real-life situations’

Article Title: BWF World Championships: For Satwiksairaj Rankireddy, Chirag Shetty’s pain is his own as the pair eyes gold
Article Text:
Chirag Shetty and Satwiksairaj Rankireddy

Satwik's new smash trick: Less shoulder, more wrist

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: For Satwiksairaj Rankireddy , injury is never a one-man problem. When his shoulder hurts, somewhere along the way, Chirag Shetty hurts too.That is the peculiar reality of a partnership that has grown far beyond the boundaries of a badminton court. The two are among India's most successful men's doubles combinations, but Satwik's recent injury layoff has also brought home just how deeply their fortunes are intertwined."It’s more tough mentally than physically to prepare,” Satwik told TOI in an interview ahead of the World Championships, beginning Aug 17. “It’s always difficult handling things which are not in your control. That was the toughest part. Few things you can’t handle. So, I think that was very frustrating and you are disturbing the other person’s life as well.”He paused to put the relationship in perspective.“When we both are healthy, both are playing good, it’s good for both. Otherwise, it’s really frustrating for the other partner.”The timing could hardly have been more cruel. After a promising start to 2026, Satwik and Chirag reached the Thailand Open final before ending a 742-day wait for a World Tour title by winning the Singapore Open.They beat world No. 1 Kim Won Ho and Seo Seung-jae in the Singapore semifinals before overcoming Fajar Alfian and Muhammad Shohibul Fikri in the final.Then came the roadblock. Satwik's recurring shoulder problem forced the pair out of the Indonesia Open and later the Japan Open, disrupting the rhythm they had painstakingly rebuilt.“I think it was difficult, but it’s part and parcel of sport. It’s how you overcome it and come back stronger,” Chirag said. “We are more than ready to do our best at the Worlds."The comeback has been deliberately cautious. Satwik and Chirag have now trained together at the Gopichand badminton academy in Hyderabad for more than a month, although Satwik initially avoided his full smash. The priority was simple: “being 100 percent injury-free and pain-free,” Chirag said.Now comes the biggest test — a home Worlds event after 17 years, where the fifth-seed, World No. 5 Indians have a first-round bye and begin in the Round of 32 against Indonesia's Ryan Indra and Nikolais Joaquin.The field is unforgiving: Korean leaders Kim Won Ho-Seo Seung-jae, Malaysia’s Aaron Chia-Soh Wooi Yik, China’s Liang Weikeng-Wang Chang and He Jiting-Ren Xiangyu, Indonesia’s Fajar-Fikri and Sabar Karyaman Gutama-Muhammad Reza Pahlevi Isfahani, Malaysia’s Goh Sze Fei-Nur Izzuddin and Japan’s Takuro Hoki-Yugo Kobayashi are among the threats.Yet Satwik refuses to look beyond the next match. “We are just focusing on ourselves,” he said. “It’s always better to take one match at a time. Not to think way, way ahead.”They already own Worlds bronze medals from 2022 and 2025. A third podium finish would further cement their place among India's badminton greats. But this time, on home soil, the ambition is bigger: to change the colour of the medal in front of a home crowd.“We can’t keep these things away...pressure of expectations would be there,” Chirag said. “But we are taking it in a positive way. People are here to support us.”And so, amid the noise, Satwik has reduced the mission to its simplest form: “My job is to focus on my rehab. Practice. Warm up. Stretching. Eat well. Sleep well. Play well. That’s it.”After the Worlds, the pair will keep their Asian Games workload selective, with Chirag confirming that the China Open will be their only tournament before the continental showpiece.Satwik’s trademark power game is getting a small but significant tweak as he returns from his shoulder injury.“I use my whole shoulder when I’m hitting the smash. Few people use only forearm and wrist and all these things. But I use my whole shoulder. So that’s why I get all the time some issues with my shoulder.”The solution is not to abandon the attacking game that has made Satwik-Chirag one of the most feared pairs in badminton, but to distribute the load better.“I have started using my wrist and forearm as well,” he said. "I'm using my shoulder and wrist and forearm. Instead of using that full shoulder, I started using other muscles as well.”For Satwik, it is a subtle adjustment aimed at making his biggest weapon more sustainable. "I’m not using the whole shoulder like I do all the time...kind of using more of the forearm and wrist.”
Article Summary: Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty are among India's most successful men's doubles combinations. Satwik's recurring shoulder problem forced the pair out of the Indonesia Open and later the Japan Open. The pair have now trained together at the Gopichand badminton academy in Hyderabad.

Article Title: India's 11 World Cup debutants: Deepika, Shilpi's remarkable journeys to Hockey's biggest stage
Article Text:

WC debutants:

When the Indian women’s team opens its World Cup campaign against China on Sunday, 11 players in the squad will be making their World Cup debuts. They come from different corners of the country — Mizoram, Jharkhand, Odisha, Haryana, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Punjab — and have taken different paths to reach hockey’s biggest stage.Some grew up with the sport, others took it up after playing different sports, while for some, hockey became a route to a better life. One of them is Jharkhand’s Deepika Soreng, who grew up in Simdega district and was introduced to hockey by Father Benedict Kujur at RC Upgraded Middle School in Karangaguri, where students were required to bring a hockey stick to school.Life, however, was far from certain. Deepika’s father died when she was a child, leaving her mother, Friska, to take up whatever work she could to support her daughter and two sons.“When I later got a chance to join the residential academy in Simdega, my mother went to Rourkela to work at the steel plant,” said Deepika, one of three students of late coach Pratima Barwa — alongside Salima Tete and Beauty Dungdung — who will play at the World Cup.Friska spent more than a decade working at the steel plant, living away from her children so they could continue their education and pursue their dreams. Years later, after Deepika broke into the national team and secured a job with the Railways, she was finally able to bring her mother back home.Friska now lives in Ranchi in her daughter’s apartment. “Next, I would like to take my mother somewhere by air. She has never travelled by flight, and I really want her to experience that at least once,” Deepika said.Because of the circumstances, Friska has not been able to follow her daughter’s hockey journey closely. She knows Deepika plays hockey and represents India, but herself knows little about the game itself. In another corner of the country, Anita Dabas, however, has closely followed her daughter Shilpi’s every step as she tried to break into the national team. A former national player from Haryana who also represented Air India, Anita made it to the India camp around 30 years ago.“She couldn’t make the team eventually. But now Shilpi has got that opportunity to represent India at the World Cup and it feels like the dream of the entire family has come true,” Shilpi’s father Anil, told TOI from their home in Sonipat. For Shilpi, the wait has been agonising. She has been playing senior nationals since 2018, but it was only earlier this year that she finally received a call-up to the senior national camp following her performance in Women’s Hockey India League with SG Pipers.“I had been trying for many years. Whenever there was a national selection or tournament, I would think, ‘Maybe my name will come this time.’ I would feel that surely it would happen now, but it just wasn’t happening,” the 28-year-old told TOI from Netherlands. There were moments of frustration, but Shilpi never stopped working. Her parents and coach Pritam Siwach ensured she kept going through the difficult years.“She would get irritated and frustrated at times. There were many occasions when I had to motivate her,” said Pritam.The persistence has now paid off. Shilpi has not only sealed her place in the World Cup squad but also played a major role in India’s Nations Cup triumph in June. Anil credits the Haryana state association and her first coach, Rajinder Singh Sr., a member of India’s 1980 Moscow Olympics gold medal-winning squad, for playing important roles in her development. Pratima did much the same for Deepika, guiding her for almost a decade before her death last year. Deepika, however, will carry her coach’s memory when she takes the field on Sunday, as will Salima and Beauty.And while they will share the same World Cup stage, the journeys that brought Deepika and Shilpi there could hardly have been more different. They were on two very different paths leading to the same dream.Lalthantluangi, Shilpi Dabas, Ishika Chaudhary, Sakshi Rana, Sunelita Toppo, Deepika Soreng, DeepikaRutuja Dadaso Pisal, Ishika, Baljeet Kaur, Beauty Dungdung

Some grew up with the sport, others took it up after playing different sports. For some, hockey became a route to a better life. Deepika Soreng's father died when she was a child.

NEW DELHI: The 65th edition of the prestigious Subroto Cup International Football Tournament will kick off on August 18, with 107 teams set to compete across three age categories in New Delhi NCR and Bengaluru.The tournament, organised by the Subroto Mukerjee Sports Education Society (SMSES) under the aegis of the Air Force Sports Control Board, will be held until Sept 24. The competition will feature Junior Girls (U-17), Sub-Junior Boys (U-15) and Junior Boys (U-17), with more than 215 matches scheduled across the three categories.The official announcement was made on Wednesday in the presence of Air Marshal S. Sivakumar VSM, Air Officer-in-Charge Administration and Vice Chairman of SMSES, who attended as the chief guest. Former India footballer Ashalata Devi Loitongbam was also present as the guest of honour.“The Indian Air Force and SMSES are committed to making the tournament bigger and better every year, providing a platform for young athletes to take the next step in their careers,” Sivakumar said.The Junior Girls (U-17) competition will open the tournament in New Delhi, NCR, from Aug 18 to 27. The Sub-Junior Boys (U-15) category will be held in Bengaluru from Sept 1 to 9, before the Junior Boys (U-17) competition concludes the tournament in New Delhi NCR from Sept 15 to 24.Teams representing various states, Union Territories and educational bodies will participate, with Sri Lanka providing international representation. An age-determination test will also be conducted for the Sub-Junior Boys category in Bengaluru to ensure a level playing field.The matches will be played at venues including Ambedkar Stadium, Tejas Football Ground, Subroto Park Football Ground, Pinto Park Football Ground and Rajokri Football Ground in the Delhi-NCR region. Article Title: MCC clarifies crucial dead-ball law following Pooran-Livingstone, Kapp-Smith incidents
Article Text:
MCC clarifies dead-ball law after contrasting incidents

What happened with Nicholas Pooran?

Why was Marizanne Kapp's delivery different?

MCC explains the law

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC) has issued an official clarification on Law 20.4.2.5 concerning batters who are not ready to face a delivery, following two contrasting incidents during The Hundred at Lord's.The clarification comes after umpires made different decisions in seemingly similar situations involving Nicholas Pooran and Marizanne Kapp . The MCC, the custodian of the Laws of Cricket, has now explained what constitutes an "attempt to play the ball" when deciding whether a delivery should be called dead.The first incident occurred during the August 6 men's fixture between MI London and London Spirit. Liam Livingstone twice stopped during his run-up before eventually delivering the ball, with Pooran indicating that he was not ready. When Livingstone bowled, Pooran withdrew his bat from the line of the delivery and made no attempt to play it. The ball hit the stumps, but umpire Mike Burns called it dead.The MCC confirmed the decision was correct, noting that Pooran had not attempted to play the ball and had adequate reason for not being ready.Three days later, a similar situation unfolded during the women's match between London Spirit and Birmingham Phoenix.Kapp appeared unprepared when Linsey Smith delivered the ball but instinctively moved her bat towards it and made contact. Umpire Mark Newell called it a fair delivery, and the MCC confirmed that decision was also correct.The MCC explained that the crucial factor is whether the batter attempted to play the ball, not whether meaningful contact was made.Under Law 20.4.2.5, a delivery can be called dead when the striker is not ready and does not attempt to play the ball, provided the umpire is satisfied that the batter had an adequate reason for being unprepared.The MCC stated: "Pooran, perhaps knowing the Law, actively withdrew his bat from the line of the ball".In Kapp's case, the governing body said she "instinctively prodded at the ball and made contact with it. As soon as she attempted to hit the ball – and note the Law talks about “attempting” to play the ball rather than actually making contact with it – the ball would not be Dead, and the ball will count in the over, as correctly identified by umpire Newell."The MCC also pointed to Law 41.10.1, which states: "It is unfair for a batter to waste time.""In the Pooran/Livingstone example, there was frustration on both sides and the natural rhythm of the over had been disrupted. Umpire Burns was correct in stating that the ball was Dead and should not count, and he would have been sensible to remind both players that the batter must not delay things and the bowler cannot overly rush things more than normal," the MCC further wrote.
Article Summary: The Marylebone Cricket Club has issued an official clarification on Law 20.4.2.5 concerning batters who are not ready to face a delivery. The clarification comes after umpires made different decisions in seemingly similar situations involving Nicholas Pooran and Marizanne Kapp. The MCC has now explained what constitutes an "attempt to play the ball" when deciding whether a delivery should be called dead.

Article Title: Canada's Harsh Thaker fined 30% of match fee for dissent during Scotland match, handed demerit points
Article Text:
Dundee, Aug 14 (IANS) Canada’s batting all-rounder Harsh Thaker has been docked 30 per cent of his match fee for showing dissent at an umpire's decision during the ICC Men’s Cricket World Cup League 2 fixture against Scotland here on Friday.

Thaker shows frustration after LBW appeal rejected

Thaker accepts sanction

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Canada suffer heavy defeat against Scotland

Canada all-rounder Harsh Thaker has been fined 30 per cent of his match fee and handed two demerit points for showing dissent at an umpire's decision during the ICC Men's Cricket World Cup League 2 fixture against Scotland in Dundee on Friday. Thaker was found to have breached Article 2.8 of the ICC Code of Conduct for Players and Player Support Personnel, which deals with showing dissent at an umpire's decision during an international match.The incident took place at the end of the 26th over when Thaker reacted angrily after the on-field umpire turned down Canada's leg-before-wicket appeal. The Canadian all-rounder flailed his arms and shook his head in disappointment. After receiving his cap back from the umpire, Thaker also gestured towards members of Canada's coaching staff, indicating that he believed the batter was out.Thaker admitted to the offence and accepted the sanction proposed by match referee Graham McCrea of the ICC International Panel of Match Referees. As a result, there was no need for a formal hearing. The charges were brought by on-field umpires Gazi Sohel and Iain McDonald, along with reserve umpire David McLean.The two demerit points mark Thaker's first offence in a 24-month period.A Level 1 breach of the ICC Code of Conduct can result in an official reprimand, a fine of up to 50 per cent of a player's match fee, and one or two demerit points. If a player accumulates four or more demerit points within a 24-month period, they are converted into suspension points. Two suspension points result in a ban from one Test, two ODIs or two T20Is, whichever comes first for the player.The disciplinary action came after a difficult outing for Canada, who suffered a heavy defeat against Scotland in the World Cup League 2 fixture. Scotland posted 347/7 before Canada were bowled out for 177, losing the match by 170 runs.
Article Summary: Canada’s batting all-rounder Harsh Thaker has been docked 30 per cent of his match fee for showing dissent at an umpire's decision. Thaker was found to have breached Article 2.8 of the ICC Code of Conduct for Players and Player Support Personnel. Article Title: Focus on Galle, eye on The Oval: 'Goal is to play WTC final,' says Shubman Gill
Article Text:
Galle: India's Captain Shubman Gill during a press conference ahead of the first Test cricket match between Sri Lanka and India, in Galle, Sri Lanka. (PTI Photo)

TimesofIndia.com

in Galle:

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India's road to the World Test Championship (WTC) final enters the home stretch from the historic city of Galle, and captain Shubman Gill has an uphill task over the next few months. The WTC final is mathematically still within India's reach but would need a performance for the ages in the next few months, starting with the series opener in Galle on August 15.The scenario is simple: win seven out of the next nine Test matches to secure the final berth. Even though the immediate challenge involves Galle, crosswinds and frequent rain interruptions, Gill and Co. have their eyes locked on the target, the "main goal"."The main goal is to play the WTC final, which is next year. And we have got about nine Tests and I think we have to win around six or seven to be able to have a good chance at qualifying. So in terms of that, I think it's a very important series for us," said Gill at the pre-match press conference.Gill is taking giant strides forward as a leader, which is reflected in how the team has prepared for the series. The captain has vocally criticised the packed scheduling and how it has robbed the side of ideal preparation before an important series in the past. Sri Lanka, on that front, has come as a breath of fresh air, as the team has been camped in Colombo since August 4, where they trained hard at the Nondescripts Cricket Club (NCC) Ground, played a warm-up fixture and squeezed in two quality sessions in Galle."If we do have an opportunity and if the scheduling allows us to have at least a week or 10 days before the Test match starts, it obviously helps with the preparation. Even last year we had quite a busy schedule in terms of, you know, travelling, playing in England and playing the Asia Cup, then playing the Test match in India, going to Australia."And then playing the Test match within four days after returning from Australia. So it's never easy for the players to be able to adapt. And most of the players in this team, I think, require a bit of time to be able to adjust to the conditions. And it's not like a lot of the players have a lot of matches or a lot of experience under their belts. So the extra time in preparation definitely helps," added Gill.Every player in the squad relies on high-volume preparation. The optional nets remained busy on the eve of the match as the likes of Gill, KL Rahul, Yashasvi Jaiswal, Ravindra Jadeja, Gurnoor Brar, Manav Suthar and others applied the finishing touches hours before taking the field in very hot and humid conditions. India's squad, hit by injury concerns, is far from the first choice, but there is no dearth of quality in the 15 assembled by the men's senior selection committee.Chairman Ajit Agarkar has been with the side in Galle, and there have been long chats involving the selector, coach and captain. For a team that has relied heavily on all-rounders to fill crucial slots, the first Test will be a rare occasion featuring more specialist players. India have been averse to compromising batting depth, even at the cost of a quality bowler, but Manav Suthar gives them the option of crucial runs and magic with the ball."He's got the ability with the bat. We know he can bat, obviously. Of course, you need a bit of experience, you need some belief and confidence. And that will only come once you're out there, you're playing, you score some runs. And hopefully he does that in the series. He's someone with great skill in bowling. And he's got the potential to be able to be a really good number 8 batsman as well," revealed Gill, all but confirming the playing XI.Both Gill and Gambhir see a lot of value in meaningful contributions from the lower order, and the captain asserts that it could seriously affect momentum and frustrate the opposition. This was the prime reason Kuldeep Yadav never made the playing XI for the five Tests in England and has often been benched for limited-overs fixtures too. In Suthar, the team is trying to plug that spot, especially in conditions where they have the option of fielding three spinners.It will be hard work for the two fast bowlers in testing conditions. While Gill didn't confirm the bowler who would partner Mohammed Siraj, he dropped enough hints that it will be difficult to look beyond Prasidh Krishna for this fixture. Additionally, Brar had a heavy workout on the eve of the match, which is not usual, especially when you are expected to undergo the grind in a few hours."They both are very skilled bowlers and they bowled really well in the practice match. We have seen how good Gurnoor is with the old ball when nothing else is happening. You need that bit of extra pace and extra bounce. He's obviously very tall as well. But I think Prasidh recently has been bowling the best that I have ever seen him bowl. In red ball and also in white ball. So it would be a very tough decision for us to pick just one," said Gill.With a fort in the backdrop, Gill will beam with pride when he walks out for the toss wearing the captain's blazer in the team's 600th Test on August 15. The spin, turn, nature of the pitch and the crosswinds can take a backseat for the moment the coin is flipped in the air because once it comes down, the business will begin.Galle will decide how much work is needed to reach The Oval.
Article Summary: India take on Sri Lanka in the first Test in Galle on August 15. Captain Shubman Gill says the team's main goal is to qualify for the World Test Championship final. India have been camped in Colombo since August 4, where they trained hard.

Article Title: 'We are in touch with them': Shubman Gill on Sai Sudharsan, Jasprit Bumrah's absence ahead of Galle Test
Article Text:
Sai Sudarshan and Jasprit Bumrah

Gill confirms constant monitoring of injured players

Five-day Test format behind selection call

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Gill backs India's bench strength

India vs Sri Lanka Test series schedule

India captain Shubman Gill has been declared fit and is ready to lead the team in the first Test against Sri Lanka, beginning in Galle on August 15. However, injuries to key players remain a concern for the Indian camp, with Jasprit Bumrah and Sai Sudharsan ruled out of the two-Test series.Bumrah, who was initially included in the squad, was ruled out due to a knee injury, while Sudharsan was sidelined with a toe niggle after failing to recover as expected. Speaking at the pre-match press conference ahead of the opening Test, Gill said the team management remains in constant touch with the injured players and is closely monitoring their fitness.“Yes, we are in touch with them. There is constant monitoring on players and where they are (in terms of fitness),” Gill said.Gill also explained Sudharsan's situation and admitted that the batter's absence was unfortunate.“Sai’s case was quite unfortunate. It looked like he would be able to be a part of the series. But we did constant scans and he wasn't improving as much as we would have liked or expected him to be,” Gill added.The India captain added that the team eventually decided not to risk Sudharsan's fitness, keeping in mind the demands of Test cricket.“So, sometimes you have to take a call from the player's point of view as to whether you want to take that risk,” he added.Gill highlighted the five-day nature of Test cricket as one of the key reasons behind the decision to leave the injured players out.“The Test match is for 5 days. If it's one-day or T20, then it's a different story. But in the Test match, you don't want to take a risk. I feel that in the Test match, you have more opportunities with other players to come back,” he explained.“For example, if you don't play well on the first day, you get another chance. So, the players have more chances to come back. So, keeping that in mind, we were a little disappointed with Sai and Bumrah.” Shubman added.Despite the absence of two important players, Gill insisted that the setbacks have not affected the team's morale. He backed the players in the squad to step up when given an opportunity.“But it didn't affect the morale of the team that much that they didn't get the first 11. I feel that whoever is in our 15 or whoever we give a chance in our playing 11 in any condition, they can play well and win the game,” Gill said.The first Test of India's two-match tour of Sri Lanka will begin on August 15 at the Galle International Cricket Stadium. The second Test is scheduled to be played at the Sinhalese Sports Club in Colombo from August 23 to 27.
Article Summary: India captain Shubman Gill has been declared fit for the first Test against Sri Lanka. Jasprit Bumrah and Sai Sudharsan have been ruled out of the two-Test series. Gill said the team management remains in constant touch with the injured players and is closely monitoring their fitness.

India captain Shubman Gill has indicated that Prasidh Krishna is likely to share the new ball with Mohammed Siraj in the first Test against Sri Lanka, which starts on Saturday. However, Gill admitted that choosing between Prasidh and uncapped pacer Gurnoor Brar is a "tough call".India are expected to field three left-arm spinners — Ravindra Jadeja and Manav Suthar as orthodox options, along with wrist-spinner Kuldeep Yadav. Article Title: Tanzid Hasan creates history in 1st Test as Bangladesh put Australia under pressure in Darwin
Article Text:
1st Test: Tanzid, Shanto (ANI Image)

Tanzid Hasan scripts history with maiden Test century

Shanto leads from the front

Australia fight back with second new ball

Bangladesh produced a dominant display on Day 2 of the first Test in Darwin, ending the day at 351/6 to establish a commanding 153-run lead over Australia. After dismissing Australia for 198 in the first innings, Bangladesh's batters made the most of favourable conditions, with opener Tanzid Hasan and captain Najmul Hossain Shanto leading the charge.Tanzid Hasan was the standout performer for Bangladesh as he scored a memorable 101 off 197 balls. The 25-year-old, playing only his second Test match, became the first Bangladeshi batter to score a Test century on Australian soil. Tanzid showed patience and discipline throughout his innings before reaching the landmark, providing Bangladesh with a strong platform at the top of the order.Captain Najmul Hossain Shanto continued Bangladesh's impressive batting effort with a crucial 84. He struck seven boundaries and a six during his composed knock before being dismissed by Josh Hazlewood. Shanto's innings ensured Bangladesh maintained their advantage even after the departure of Tanzid.Mominul Haque also made a valuable contribution but narrowly missed out on a half-century. Resuming his innings from his overnight score, Mominul was dismissed by Hazlewood for 49, falling just one run short of the milestone.Hazlewood was Australia's most effective bowler alongside Mitchell Starc as the hosts attempted to make a late comeback.Australia finally managed to put some pressure on Bangladesh late in the day. The introduction of the second new ball triggered a mini-collapse, with Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Pat Cummins taking three wickets for just 11 runs. Starc finished with figures of 2/68, Hazlewood also claimed 2/68, while Cummins took 1/50.Bangladesh's lower order showed resilience to ensure Australia did not completely seize the momentum. Mehidy Hasan Miraz remained unbeaten on 32, while Hasan Mahmud was 13 not out at stumps. The pair helped Bangladesh safely negotiate the closing stages and ensured the visitors retained a sizeable advantage heading into Day 3.With a 153-run lead and four wickets still in hand, Bangladesh will look to stretch their advantage further on Day 3 and put Australia under even greater pressure.
Article Summary: Bangladesh reach 351-6 on Day 2 of the first Test in Darwin. Opener Tanzid Hasan scored a memorable 101 off 197 balls. Captain Najmul Hossain Shanto made 84 before being dismissed by Josh Hazlewood. Australia took three wickets for just 11 runs in the final hour of the day.

NEW DELHI: Tripura chief minister Manik Saha has fulfilled a promise made to Commonwealth Games gold medallist Asmita Dey, with the state government allotting her a piece of land in Agartala to build a house.The 23-year-old judoka was honoured in Tripura on Wednesday after becoming the first Indian judoka to win a Commonwealth Games gold medal.Dey won the women’s -48kg title in Glasgow after defeating Canada’s Heidi Quach in a dramatic golden-score contest. Article Title: Rajasthan stuck in 2012, Manipur in 2023: How actively are states with CWG medals promoting sports?
Article Text:
Are sports bodies of Indian states promoting the game properly?

Haryana: Hit on the podium, not so much off it

Manipur still talking about 2023

Rajasthan: 14 years and counting

And then come Tamil Nadu and others

The ones somewhere in the middle

Does it matter so much?

NEW DELHI: Somewhere on a muddy school field in Haryana right now, a teenager is perhaps drilling the same throwing technique over and over, just as she had watched on television just days ago. Her sole aim is to pull off the one like Sharmila Dhankar, India's Commonwealth Games shot put gold medallist.Before the 2026 CWG campaign, she, like many of us, had almost certainly never heard the name. And it's not because Dhankar had not won anything before the Glasgow Games; she had, a gold medal in the Women's Shot Put F57 event at the 2026 Fazza International Para Athletics Championship, but because one of the primary institutions whose entire job was to carry that story back from the medal podium to villages and training grounds across the state has, for all practical purposes, gone quiet.That's the part of this story that rarely gets told. India walked away from Glasgow with 39 medals, and for a week, the athletes who won them were everywhere, garlanded at airports, seated beside ministers, their faces on the evening news. But medals don't build the next generation of athletes by themselves. Somebody has to keep telling their stories, long after the felicitation photo is filed away, to the kid training in a dusty school ground who needs proof that this path actually leads somewhere.We wanted to know which state sports departments are still doing their job of promoting the sports and their grassroots on their social media platforms, and which ones seem to have simply logged off. So we scrolled through the timelines ourselves. Here's what we found.No state produced more glory in Glasgow than Haryana. Eleven medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze, spanning boxing, wrestling, athletics, and para sport, headlined by a Neeraj Chopra silver that will be replayed on sports channels for years.Alongside him were names most of India still had little knowledge of. The likes of Preeti Pawar, Jaismine Lamboria, Sakshi Chaudhary, Priya Ghanghas, Sachin Siwach, and Ankush Panghal, all of whom trained in government facilities, under government schemes, and who'd probably appreciate their own state department cheering as loudly for them as it does for its concert lineups.Because that's the thing. The Sports Department, Government of Haryana's X account has posted exactly once in all of 2026, and it's a flyer for the music acts playing at the Chief Minister's Cup.Facebook and Instagram follow a similar rhythm with a short cluster of posts around that February event, and then not much else.Eleven medals, and not one dedicated post to show for it. Somewhere in Rohtak or Bhiwani, a young pugilist training in Priya Ghanghas's discipline would probably just like a little proof that someone up top is paying attention.Manipur's page has an odd time-capsule quality to it. This is the state that gave India Mirabai Chanu, one of the country's most beloved Olympic medalists, and this Commonwealth Games alone produced four medalists from Manipur, Chanu's gold among them, alongside Rishikanta Singh, Bindyarani Devi, and Jadumani Singh.And yet the Department of Youth Affairs & Sports' X account hasn't posted since October 2023, a "Run for Unity" event, frozen well before any of this year's medals happened.Although the Facebook page has had a few sporadic posts here and there this year, its Instagram account has managed just two posts since January. It’s the kind of gap that makes you wonder if someone simply forgot the login details somewhere along the way.If there's one number in this whole exercise worth sitting with, it's this: the official Sports Department, Government of Rajasthan hasn't posted on Facebook since April 14, 2012.Fourteen years, through Arundhati Choudhary's Commonwealth gold and everything else that's happened in Rajasthan sport since.Its X account's last original post predates a retweet from March 2021, and there's no Instagram at all. A parallel handle, the Rajasthan State Sports Council, exists across all three platforms and is barely livelier.Somewhere behind Choudhary's medal is a genuinely good story, but it just hasn't found a home on the one page built to tell it.Gulveer Singh managed both a silver and a bronze for Uttar Pradesh this Games, a rare double that would make a great centrepiece for the state's sporting year. Instead, across two separate official handles on three platforms, Uttar Pradesh Sports has produced little beyond reposts, while its sister account, Sports Directorate, Govt of Uttar Pradesh, hasn't posted at all in 2026.Delhi Government, for its part, doesn't run a dedicated sports account at all on any of the popular social media platforms, so gold medalist Harsh Singh and bronze medalist Tejaswin Shankar, both representing India's capital, don't really have an institutional cheerleader online, their wins quietly absorbed into the general churn of city government updates. Both athletes are, in effect, doing their own promotional legwork.Set against all that quiet, Tamil Nadu feels like a different sport altogether. Its Sports Tamil Nadu handles post multiple times a day, celebrating not just its own three medalists, Praveen Chithravel, Selva Prabhu, Muthupandi Raja, but athletes from other states too, weaving in government scheme updates without it ever reading like bureaucracy.Every medallist got a dedicated post. Somewhere in Tamil Nadu, a kid training in long jump or wrestling doesn't have to wonder whether the sport leads anywhere. The state tells them, publicly, almost daily.Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka's Facebook and Instagram pages, Assam, Bihar, and Tripura all follow a version of that same habit, active, consistent, generous with attention toward athletes nobody outside their district would otherwise know existed.Kerala doesn't run a separate sports handle on X but keeps its Facebook and Instagram genuinely lively, making sure Murali Sreeshankar and Mohammed Basil's silvers got their due.Andhra Pradesh mirrors that same rhythm across all three platforms.Not every state falls neatly into being inactive or staying proactive. Punjab's account managed just two posts on X all year, New Year's and Republic Day, though its Facebook and Instagram carry a bit more life around coaching and departmental meetings, even if athletes rarely get top billing.Uttarakhand was genuinely active last year before cooling off in 2026, leaning more toward government scheme announcements on Facebook, though its Instagram at least carried two posts around the Games.Maharashtra has dedicated posts up for both Sarvesh Kushare and Dilip Gavit, with Instagram staying fairly regular, enough effort to stay out of the quiet column.Karnataka's X account hasn't posted since March 2024, around an unrelated cultural-team event, even though its Facebook and Instagram have stayed warm and active toward its CWG medalists.It is worth asking why this actually matters, beyond good manners. Well, a state sports department's social media feed isn't just a courtesy board for congratulations; it's one of the cheapest, most direct tools available to build the next generation of athletes.A youngster in a small town is far more likely to pick up a javelin because they saw a state government post celebrating someone from their own district. Even when it comes to promoting any government policy, social media can be as effective.Visibility drives aspiration. There's a funding logic too. Sponsors, corporates, and even state finance departments allocate resources partly based on visible public interest, and a well-run social account is often the easiest evidence a sport has that interest.ALSO READ: Anahat Singh: What is in the name? A word from Guru Nanak's prayer, now India's squash sensation Silence, on the other hand, sends the message that grassroots sport isn't a priority worth the effort of a single post, even when the state has just produced a medallist on the world stage.It is worth it because sometimes, the first step towards building a sporting culture is simply showing people that their achievements are being seen.
Article Summary: India won 39 medals at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Haryana produced 11 medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze. But the state sports department has posted just once in all of 2026. What do you think is more important for grassroots sports promotion? Government funding or social media presence? Share your view.

Article Title: ‘That video was not ordinary’: PM Modi praises Lovlina for objecting to distorted India map - Watch
Article Text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi shares a light moment with boxer Lovlina Borgohain. (PTI Photo)

‘That video was not ordinary’

Mirabai opens up about four difficult years

Narender's joke leaves Modi laughing

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Boxer Lovlina Borgohain's decision to object to a distorted Indian map during the Commonwealth Games earned special appreciation from Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time.Lovlina, who won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow, was among India's medal winners who interacted with Modi at his residence on Sunday. The meeting, attended by Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya, Minister of State for Sports Raksha Khadse and Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha, saw athletes recount their experiences from the Games in an informal and emotional setting.In a little over 10-minute video of the interaction shared by the Prime Minister's Office on Monday, Modi brought up Lovlina's confrontation with a restaurant in Glasgow after she noticed a distorted Indian map.“Kya hua wo restaurant waale se jhagda kar rahi thi? (What happened, you were fighting with that restaurant guy?)” Modi asked.Lovlina laughed before explaining why she intervened.“We had such a good performance and it was the last day of the Games. It was a happy occasion sir, we were celebrating and I didn't like it when I saw the distorted map. I politely told them and they have made the changes also,” she explained.Modi applauded the boxer for noticing the issue despite being in the middle of celebrations after her medal-winning campaign.“To be able to recognise the significance of that map at a time when you were celebrating and the Games were over, I can tell you truthfully, that video was not ordinary. It will be remembered by people for a very long time,” he told the Tokyo Olympics bronze medallist.India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.The interaction also provided an emotional window into Mirabai Chanu's journey to her gold medal in the women's 48kg category. The weightlifter produced a Games-record lift of 190kg, but her triumph came after four difficult years following her one-kilogram miss at the Paris Olympics. Modi asked Mirabai about the tears she shed on the podium and even fed her a laddu during their interaction.“Itne aansu tapak rahe the (So many tears were rolling down),” Modi remarked.Mirabai explained that the tears represented years of accumulated emotions.“I was very happy and emotional at that moment. I was crying because I missed a medal in the Paris Olympics by one kilogram. I have faced a lot in these last four years. I was battling injuries and some family problems too.“There were a lot of things. So, these four years were very tough for me. And when I stood on the podium, our flag went up and the anthem played, it was hard to stop myself,” she said.The meeting also had its lighter moments. Boxer Narender Berwal, who won silver in the +90kg category, recalled a funny exchange with a Pakistani boxer after beating him at the 2015 World Military Games.“During the 2015 World Military Games, I had a bout with a Pakistani boxer. I won it but when we were together in the medical room for treatment to our niggles, he said to me 'Bhaijan aapka naam Narender hai, aapke coach ka naam Narender hai, aapke Pradhan Mantri ka naam Narender hai, mujhe Narender naam se nafrat ho gayi hai.' (Brother, you, your coach and your PM are all named Narender. I hate this name now),” he recalled, drawing laughter from Modi.The Prime Minister also underlined the broader significance of the athletes' achievements, saying their medals were helping inspire a new generation.“I have been in this house for 12-13 years now and if there is one group that I have met regularly here, it is the athletes because of your efforts to win medals for India and your tradition of scaling new heights.“Far more than our push to promote sports in schools, it is your medals that inspire people,” Modi said.

Article Title: ‘From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping’: PM Modi’s heartfelt message to CWG heroes - Watch

NEW DELHI: “From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping.”Prime Minister Narendra Modi had an emotional message for Mirabai Chanu as he interacted with India's Commonwealth Games 2026 medal winners at his residence on Sunday, reflecting on the sacrifices behind the country's successful campaign in Glasgow.Modi hosted the medal-winning contingent at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg and heard athletes recount some of the moments that defined their journeys at the Games. India returned from Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze, finishing fourth in the overall standings.During one of the conversations, Modi recalled the emotional scenes surrounding Mirabai's gold-medal triumph.“Tears were falling from you. I feel as if from every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping,” Modi told the Olympic silver medallist.Mirabai, who won gold in Glasgow, opened up about the difficult journey that preceded her Commonwealth Games triumph, including the disappointment of the Paris Olympics.“I was very happy, and emotional too. That day the happiness was greater and I cried because at the Paris Olympics, I lost a medal by 1 kg. In a player’s life what all we have to face. So within these 4 years, how much and what all I had faced, every time injuries were going on and all that was happening.So with great difficulty I had faced these 4 years. So when all that happened, on the podium when I stood, sir, and when our flag goes up and our national anthem plays, sir, we cannot stop, sir, tears come out on their own,” she said.Modi responded by highlighting the wider impact of the athletes' achievements.“This is very good. It is not as if this achievement of yours is considered only your achievement; your victory becomes a very big inspiration for the coming generations.”The informal interaction also saw athletes share lighter and deeply personal moments from their Glasgow campaigns.Modi reminded para shot put gold medallist Sharmila Dhankar of a promise she had made earlier.“You made a promise. Last time, yours, both daughters will become players,” Modi said with a smile.Dhankar replied: “Haanji, right now they are young in age. In the next Commonwealth, one family will bring 3 medals.”Men's 100m T47 gold medallist Dilip Gavit, meanwhile, spoke about dedicating his performance to his guru.“When I was running, when my event was on 29th (July), that day was Guru Purnima, so that day I gave a gift to my guru,” he was heard saying in the video.In another video posted by Modi, gold medallist boxer Sakshi Chaudhary introduced herself and the contingent.“Hello friends! This is Sakshi Chaudhary. Today, our honourable Prime Minister has invited us, the Commonwealth Games medalists, and we feel very proud. We are extremely happy to have met him; he is very humble. Sir, would you like to say something?” she said.Modi replied with a message that summed up his interaction with the athletes: “Jo khelega, woh khilega” (The one who plays, will blossom). “Always cheer for Bharat.”India's fourth-place finish came despite a significantly smaller contingent and a reduced sporting programme compared to Birmingham 2022. India sent 122 athletes to Glasgow, compared to 210 in Birmingham, while 30 of its 61 medals in 2022 came in sports that were not part of the Glasgow programme.Despite those limitations, India retained its fourth-place position and improved its medal conversion rate, with 38 athletes returning home with medals.
